title: The FREEZER role's only power is revoking a relayer, separating emergency response from both operations and configuration
content:
A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.1.2.1.3 introduces the freezer functions of the `MainnetController`, and A...3.1 through A...3.1.3 show the entire surface: `removeRelayer(address relayer) external onlyRole(FREEZER)`, whose body is `_revokeRole(RELAYER, relayer)` followed by `emit RelayerRemoved(relayer)`.

Grove therefore runs a clean three-way separation. `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` sets parameters — mint recipients, max slippage, tick bounds, TWAP windows, the Merkl distributor (A...3.1.1 through A...3.1.10). `RELAYER` executes operations within those parameters. `FREEZER` can do exactly one thing: take the relayer's keys away.

The asymmetry is the design. Emergency response needs to be fast, so the freezer should be held by an entity that can act without deliberation — and that is only safe if the role is **purely subtractive**. A freezer cannot appoint a replacement relayer, cannot redirect funds, and cannot loosen a limit, so compromising the freezer key buys an attacker a denial of service and nothing more.

The corresponding cost is that freezing is not a pause: outstanding approvals granted by earlier relayer actions survive revocation, and anything already delegated — an Ethena signer (A...10.1), a Merkl operator (A...14.1) — remains authorised, because revoking those requires a relayer. The freezer stops new actions; it does not unwind standing authority.
description: removeRelayer calls _revokeRole(RELAYER, relayer) and emits an event — nothing else; the freezer cannot move funds, set parameters, or appoint anyone.
